idiom_name: Rack::Attack throttle rules over a cache store (Redis/Memcached for multi-process)
implementation_notes: Ruby's conventional realization for HTTP traffic is Rack::Attack: named throttle rules (Rack::Attack.throttle('logins/ip', limit: 5, period: 60) { |req| ... }) count matching requests per key in a cache store and answer 429 once the limit is exceeded, with safelists taking precedence and fail2ban/allow2ban patterns for harsher cases. The store is the correctness boundary - the Rails cache (often a per-process MemoryStore in development, Redis in production) decides whether the limit holds across workers - and throttled_responder customizes the refusal body, status and headers. Outside Rack there is no core limiter; a token bucket over Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC) and a Mutex is the hand-rolled fallback.
pitfalls: The default Rack::Attack cache in development and test is process-local; the same rules undercount once several Puma workers or hosts run.
Rules are evaluated per request in middleware - an expensive block (deep parsing, uncached lookups) makes the throttle itself the bottleneck.
Throttle counters inherit the cache store's eviction semantics; an evicted counter silently resets the window.
